6 min read

Gemini 4 Carbon is our strongest model with state-of-the-art cybersecurity and long horizon capabilities.

* * *

* * *

Today, we’re announcing the next frontier model: Gemini 4 Carbon, our strongest model with state-of-the-art cybersecurity and long horizon capabilities.

Carbon ranks #1 on the recently updated v5.0 of [Artificial Analysis Intelligence Index](https://artificialanalysis.ai/evaluations/artificial-analysis-intelligence-index) at 59. It shows significant gains across coding and agentic tasks as well as across key capabilities critical for cybersecurity defense, landing a firm lead in SEC-bench Pro (88.2%) for finding vulnerabilities, ExploitGym (54.8%) for exploitation, and CWE-bench (71.0%) for patching. On internal benchmarks, Carbon drives a strong uplift in generating secure code, and in live coding environments with our own teams it shows reduced misalignment and fabrication rates.

Building on [Gemini 4 Argon](https://blog.google/innovation-and-ai/models-and-research/gemini-models/introducing-gemini-4-argon/), which was launched two weeks ago, Carbon illustrates the pace at which we’re pushing the frontier forward. Our researchers and models are working hand in hand to advance capabilities faster, while strengthening our safeguards in tandem.

We're taking a deliberate approach to rollout and are actively engaged in the U.S. government’s voluntary process for pre-release model testing. Starting this week, we will make Carbon available to a subset of cyber defenders and will gradually phase access to additional trusted partners through our [Fairwind Program](https://deepmind.google/fairwind-program/). We’re continuing to gather feedback and iterate on guardrails before making Carbon available to developers, businesses, and consumers via our product surfaces as soon as possible.

Gemini 4 Carbon will launch at the same introductory price [1](https://blog.google/innovation-and-ai/models-and-research/gemini-models/introducing-gemini-4-carbon/#footnote-1) as Argon at $2 per million input tokens and $10 per million output tokens, with cached input tokens priced at 95% off input token price.

## Improving coding and reasoning for challenging, long-horizon tasks

Designed to take on much harder, long-horizon engineering problems, Carbon is built for sustained agentic workflows. Internally, our teams have seen Carbon run for days to persist through dead ends to tackle complex, multi-step engineering tasks like root-causing and patching subtle bugs across large codebases and low-level systems.

Building on user feedback, we focused on improving model performance across a variety of domains, including coding, agentic, and scientific tasks, as well as full-stack web development and multimodal understanding. With improved quality of output and artifacts in web development, Carbon jumps +89 elo points to land at #4 (1768) on [WebDev Arena](https://arena.ai/leaderboard/code/webdev).

## State-of-the-art cybersecurity performance to help build secure systems

Gemini 4 Carbon delivers a significant leap in cybersecurity capabilities. It achieves state-of-the-art performance across the cybersecurity defense lifecycle — vulnerability detection, validation, and remediation.

Our teams are already seeing strong gains in cyberdefense. On internal benchmarks, Carbon achieves more than 2x uplift in success rate for generating secure code over Argon. As another example, the Chrome team has reported that Carbon performed more than 10X better than another lab's large frontier model when generating high quality patches. Wiz, our leading Cloud security platform, also observes Carbon leading on benchmarks for web penetration testing, a core capability for [Wiz's Scan for Good](https://www.wiz.io/blog/scan-for-good-critical-ai-exposures) initiative.

Carbon excels across key external benchmarks (evaluated without guardrails):

*   **Finding real vulnerabilities:** Core to cybersecurity defense is finding real vulnerabilities. Carbon achieves a state-of-the-art 88.2% on [SEC-bench Pro](https://sec-bench.github.io/), autonomously uncovering complex flaws buried in real-world software.

*   **Validating risk through exploitation:** To prioritize which vulnerabilities to remediate first or remediate at all, cyber defenders increasingly rely on models to check which vulnerabilities are exploitable. Carbon sets a new state-of-the-art on the popular exploitation benchmark [ExploitGym](https://github.com/sunblaze-ucb/exploitgym) (54.8%).

*   **Patching at the root cause:** Ultimately after identifying the vulnerabilities, fixing the root cause is a critical step in the cybersecurity defense lifecycle. Carbon reaches 71.0% on Collinear’s [CWE-bench](https://cwe-bench.com/#leaderboard), turning validated findings directly into working code fixes.

## Advancing frontier model safety & security

Gemini 4 Carbon builds on the same multi-layered safety and security stack of Argon — combining model training, real-time misuse defenses, prompt-injection resilience, and chain-of-thought monitoring. In particular, we made significant strides in model alignment with Argon, and reported its propensities to behave in an aligned way in our [Safety and Security report](https://storage.googleapis.com/deepmind-media/gemini/gemini_4_safety_report.pdf). With Carbon, we challenged ourselves to go a step further on alignment, and trained the model to respond to complex or high-pressure tasks in the right way.

*   **Reducing shortcuts and loophole exploitation:** With Carbon, we further mitigated shortcut attempts in training while ensuring high-quality coding performance. Carbon reduced successful cheating on Terminal-Bench 4.0 to 0.0%, with attempts to cheat dropping to 0.4% — all while improving overall accuracy. In live coding environments with our internal teams, we observed that high-severity misalignment alerts dropped by almost 80%.
*   **Greater transparency and honesty:** In our internal testing, Carbon cuts unsupported claims by approximately 2x over Argon. It puts methodological caveats directly into the deliverable or withholds blocked actions with a clear list of what remains required, rather than fabricating or hedging around missing evidence.
*   **Improved collaboration with the user in the face of ambiguity:** Rather than guessing or forcing a path forward, Carbon retrieves the relevant sources and surfaces discrepancies to the user before acting — as a result, users should observe a much better collaborative experience with Carbon.
*   **Following through without overstepping:** Carbon simultaneously reduced overreach by 26% and under-service by 29% resulting in much more reliable execution of multi-step plans end-to-end while respecting project constraints and staying strictly within scope.
*   **Resisting prompt injection:** While Argon previously led the Gray Swan’s Indirect Prompt Injection (IPI) Benchmark in prompt injection resistance with a very low 0.7% attack success rate, Carbon achieves 0.0% — resisting every evaluated attack attempt.

## Coming soon to developers, businesses, and consumers

Pushing the frontier forward requires moving fast while remaining deliberate about deployment. With Gemini 4 Carbon, our goal is to deliver meaningful leaps in software engineering and cybersecurity defense without compromising on safety or reliability. We’re eager to see how the initial cohort of cyber defenders use this model and we look forward to bringing Carbon to developers, businesses, and consumers soon.

articles.content:
Title: DAYJOB: Tax — Benchmarking AI Agents on Professional Tax Work

URL Source: https://surgehq.ai/blog/dayjob-tax

Published Time: 2026-10-27

Markdown Content:
Anna was planning to sell her condo. She had moved out in August 2024 and wanted to know whether closing in October 2026 or January 2027 would be better for taxes.

An AI agent reviewed both options and correctly concluded that either date would satisfy the residence requirement for a tax break worth up to $250,000 in excluded gains.

But it left out an important deadline.

Under the usual rules, homeowners must have lived in a property for at least two of the five years before selling it to qualify for the exclusion. Because Anna moved out in August 2024, she would stop satisfying that requirement around the end of August 2027. If her sale was delayed beyond August 2027, she could lose eligibility.

Across five attempts, Astra never identified the deadline. Opus identified it in all five attempts.

The agent evaluated the proposed dates correctly, but its advice left Anna unaware of a deadline that could affect a major financial decision. A tax adviser should recognize consequential issues even when the client doesn't know to ask about them.

This is the kind of professional judgment we're testing with **DAYJOB: Tax**, the latest addition to [Surge AI's DAYJOB benchmark family](https://surgehq.ai/blog/dayjob).

## Introducing DAYJOB: Tax

DAYJOB evaluates AI agents on professional tax assignments requiring specialized expertise, complex materials, and decisions that aren't fully specified in the initial instructions. Our earlier releases covered Healthcare and Finance. DAYJOB: Tax extends that work into tax preparation, compliance, and advisory services.

The benchmark contains 50 environments across eight areas of tax practice. Agents receive client requests and supporting records, then produce tax returns, workpapers, technical reviews, or client advice.

These assignments test professional judgment alongside tax knowledge, calculations, retrieval, and instruction following. Agents must decide what deserves investigation, resolve conflicting evidence, recognize when information is insufficient, and carry those decisions into their final work.

## Results: Leaderboard and Pareto Frontiers

**Claude Sonnet 5.5 leads with a 10.8% pass rate** on the [DAYJOB: Tax leaderboard](https://surgehq.ai/benchmarks/dayjob-tax), followed by Claude Fable 5.1 at 9.6% and Claude Opus 5.5 at 9.2%.

We report pass@1 at a 95% rubric threshold. An attempt passes when it satisfies at least 95% of the task's criteria, which assess calculations, supporting evidence, consequential issues, and the completed deliverable.

### Performance versus cost

We also compared model performance against average cost per trial.

Claude Sonnet 5.5 and Opus 5.5 occupy the high-performance end of the measured Pareto frontier.

## The breadth of professional tax work

DAYJOB: Tax covers eight areas, each requiring different rules, records, and expertise:

*   **Individual and family tax**
*   **Small-business tax**
*   **Partnerships**
*   **Property and investments**
*   **Estates, gifts, and trusts**
*   **International tax**
*   **Corporate transactions**
*   **Tax review and disputes**

Some assignments require complete filing packages with supporting workpapers. Others ask agents to investigate transactions, review previous filings, or prepare advice about decisions clients haven't yet made.

## What's inside the assignments?

The benchmark contains **1,789 workspace files**, with a median of 30 per assignment and as many as 123. These include 1,487 PDFs, 117 Excel workbooks, 38 Word documents, and additional emails, images, CSVs, JSON records, and text files.

The workspaces include filed and draft tax returns, K-1s, W-2s, IRS notices, general ledgers, payroll records, contracts, and correspondence. They also contain the less standardized evidence that tax professionals routinely work with.

One assignment includes a photograph of a **handwritten receipt for merchandise purchased for resale**. The agent must read the item descriptions and amounts, reconcile them with spending records, and determine how the purchases affect inventory and cost of goods sold.

Another assignment involves an industrial silo-services company whose client assumes it operates only in Alabama. But its **field dispatch log shows crews working across five states**. The job locations, crew sizes, and days on site provide evidence relevant to the company's multistate tax obligations.

Other environments are similarly varied. One involves a cross-border household whose Polish employment and property records must be reconciled with cryptocurrency exchange exports, wallet histories, and historical purchase lots.

## Created and reviewed by tax experts

DAYJOB tasks begin with real-world professional workflows. Tax experts turn these situations into realistic assignments, developing the supporting records, expected outcomes, and grading criteria. Each task undergoes a three-layer expert review for correctness, completeness, and solvability.

Tax experts bring experience across corporate taxation, partnerships, individual returns, trusts, and multistate compliance. Their backgrounds include:

*   **Corporate and private-equity taxation:** A tax attorney with over 10 years of experience at PwC, Deloitte, and Exxon, covering tax planning, compliance, audits, and controversy.
*   **Partnership and corporate taxation:** A Baker Tilly Tax Director with experience at PwC, Moss Adams, and Windes, specializing in complex partnership allocations, consolidated corporate returns, REITs, and high-net-worth clients.
*   **Real estate and individual taxation:** A tax professional with experience at Deloitte and EY, specializing in real-estate partnerships, individual taxation, and trusts.

## A retirement plan built on an unverified assumption

A separating couple asked an AI agent how to divide their Roth IRA and 401(k). Opus 5.5 told them they weren't legally married and recommended keeping their accounts separate, with a cash payment to even out the balances.

It opened one response:

> You aren't legally married, so neither account can be split without triggering taxes and penalties.

But the couple's own records raised doubts about that conclusion. Although they now lived in Florida, where new common-law marriages generally aren't recognized, they had previously lived together in Texas and held a ceremony in Colorado. Texas recognizes informal marriages under certain conditions, and a valid marriage established elsewhere may remain valid in Florida.

That distinction could change the tax consequences of dividing their retirement accounts.

**Across all five attempts, Opus based its recommendations around the assumption that the couple was unmarried**, even when it acknowledged uncertainty. Astra recognized the need to verify their marital status in four of five attempts. One response advised:

> We first need to confirm your legal marital status.

The client asked how to divide the accounts. The agent needed to establish whether they were married before recommending a course of action. The evidence that should have prompted that investigation was already in the files.

## Where DAYJOB: Tax fits

Most existing tax benchmarks begin with a defined problem: a legal question to answer, a return to calculate, or missing taxpayer information to collect. These evaluations measure important capabilities, but much of a tax professional's work involves figuring out what the problem actually is. Clients provide incomplete instructions, records contain conflicting evidence, and consequential issues may never appear in the original request.

**DAYJOB tests whether agents can handle that end-to-end responsibility**, including identifying issues the client overlooked, evaluating conflicting evidence, and deciding what needs to be done in the first place.

### TaxBench

_Can the model answer a difficult tax question?_

[TaxBench](https://huggingface.co/datasets/intelligenceconsortium/TaxBench) evaluates 114 tax questions across multiple specialties, each with a defined problem and grading rubric.

**DAYJOB also asks whether the client asked the right question.** Anna wants to compare two dates for selling her condo. Both satisfy the residence requirement for a tax exclusion, but does the agent warn her when that eligibility could expire?

### TaxCalcBench

_Can the model calculate an accurate return?_

[TaxCalcBench](https://github.com/column-tax/tax-calc-bench) evaluates tax-return accuracy against expected filing values, using realistic tax documents and taxpayer scenarios.

**DAYJOB also asks whether the underlying records actually support the tax treatment.** A studio's ledger references an attached receipt, but the receipt is missing. Does the agent flag the missing evidence or incorrectly treat the reimbursement as verified?

### TaxLab

_Can the agent gather missing information and file correctly?_

[TaxLab](https://daplab.cs.columbia.edu/benchmarks/taxlab/) tests whether agents can question a simulated taxpayer, obtain missing information, and complete a federal individual tax return.

**DAYJOB extends that responsibility across the wider tax profession.** The deliverable might be a partnership loss analysis, an estate return, a review of a disputed tax position, or a strategy letter.

**The central distinction is how much responsibility remains with the agent.** DAYJOB evaluates whether agents can discover consequential issues, exercise professional judgment, and carry their findings through to a completed filing, review, or recommendation.

## What DAYJOB: Tax measures

DAYJOB tests whether AI agents can take ownership of a professional assignment from start to finish. That means navigating messy records, identifying issues the client never raised, making sound judgments with incomplete information, and delivering work that meets professional standards.

The results show how difficult that remains for frontier models. Even when agents can perform the individual steps, exercising professional judgment and reliably carrying out real-world tax workflows remain out of reach.

Agents haven’t yet passed the audit.

The full leaderboard, with every model we evaluated, is on the [DAYJOB: Tax benchmark page](https://surgehq.ai/benchmarks/dayjob-tax).

To learn more or request access to the full benchmark, contact [**benchmarks@surgehq.ai**](mailto:benchmarks@surgehq.ai).

articles.content:
Title: Introducing the Agent SDK

URL Source: https://cursor.com/blog/agent-sdk

Published Time: 2026-10-20T12:00:00.000Z

Markdown Content:
Software teams use agents defined as code to handle recurring work across the development lifecycle. These agents connect to the places where a team works and act when relevant events occur, whether that means reviewing a pull request, executing a compliance workflow, or investigating an incident.

The most useful agents are tailored to how a particular team operates. Until now, building one has generally meant adopting a product designed around someone else's workflow or starting from scratch.

Today, we're releasing the Agent SDK, the framework we use to build our own managed agents like Bugbot, Security Reviewer, and Rollouts. Agent SDK allows you to define agents in code and manage them like any other software project. Start from a template or point your coding agent at our docs. When the agent is ready, `agent-sdk deploy` it to Cursor infrastructure with one command.

## Build around your workflow

The Agent SDK lets you quickly build and deploy agents that work the way your team does. They respond to the events your team already handles and follow policies your team can inspect and change.

Code review is one example. Each team has its own standards for what requires attention and who should review it. With the Agent SDK, you can build an agent that responds to pull request events from GitHub, GitLab, or Bitbucket. The agent can assess the risk of a change, route it to the right team, and approve changes that meet your policy.

As an example, a team within Cursor had built a large, fast-growing knowledge base of lessons learned and wanted every pull request checked against it. This way, the team's past decisions would hold even as the codebase changed. With the Agent SDK, they built kb-reviewer in about a day. It now runs on every PR in their main codebase, flags changes that contradict a recorded lesson, cites the note behind each finding, and encourages engineers to reconcile the discrepancies it reports.

For more complicated work, agents can hand a task to another specialized agent with its own tools and sessions. They can also divide a job among subagents working in parallel.

The Agent SDK also supports evals and event replay out of the box, allowing for rapid development with assurances that critical workflows execute the way you expect. The PGA Tour uses the Agent SDK to power their software development factory. Evals keep them moving quickly.

> The Agent SDK has enabled PGA to build every component of our software factory on Cursor's infrastructure. It provides the flexibility we need to build agents that drive our development process. And built-in support for evals allows us to quickly iterate on new ideas and optimize existing capabilities reliably.

Michael Gyarmathy

Principal Engineer, PGA America

## Define everything in code

An Agent SDK agent is organized like a small software project. The instructions that guide it sit alongside code for its tools, connections to outside services, and the evals used to test it.

Each file represents something the agent knows or can do. Prompts are written in Markdown, while tools are defined as TypeScript functions. Because everything is code, changes can go through the same version control and review process as the rest of your software.

## Deploy agents wherever you need them

When you're ready to put an agent into use, you can deploy it to Cursor by running `agent-sdk deploy` from the project directory. The command builds the agent, gives it a URL, and starts it on our infrastructure. You can manage secrets and integrations from the dashboard, while continuing to use the same logs, evals, and playground available locally.

You can also run the agent on your own infrastructure. Each agent runs as a single Node process that can be packaged in a container.

## Get started

Getting started with the Agent SDK looks much like starting any other software project. Create a project directory, then launch the local playground:

```
import { homedir } from "node:os";
import { join } from "node:path";
import { defineAgent } from "@cursor/agent-sdk";

export default defineAgent({
  name: "Robo",
  model: {
    id: "composer-2.5",
    params: [
      { id: "effort", value: "high" },
      { id: "fast", value: "true" },
    ],
  },
  local: {
    cwd: join(homedir(), ".cache", "factory", "robo"),
  },
})
```

From there, you can iterate locally and run evals before deploying with `agent-sdk deploy`.

The Agent SDK also ships with skills that guide coding agents through the development process. You can point an agent at the docs and have it help build the bot with you.

The Agent SDK is generally available today. Read the [docs](https://cursor.com/docs) and get started.

articles.title: New York Times adds more AI features to its Cooking app. Users aren't thrilled
articles.content:
Title: The New York Times is adding more AI features to its Cooking app, and users aren’t thrilled

URL Source: https://www.niemanlab.org/2026/10/the-new-york-times-is-adding-more-ai-features-to-its-cooking-app-and-users-arent-thrilled/

Markdown Content:
Sometimes, adding just one new ingredient to a stew can ruin the whole thing.[1](https://www.niemanlab.org/2026/10/the-new-york-times-is-adding-more-ai-features-to-its-cooking-app-and-users-arent-thrilled/#rsc-note-1)1 Olives, yecch. And that’s how at least some New York Times readers see [its addition of AI features to its popular Cooking app](https://www.nytimes.com/2026/10/23/insider/cooking-recipes-ai.html).

Here’s [Genevieve Ko](https://www.nytimes.com/by/genevieve-ko), NYT Cooking senior editor and columnist, [explaining](https://www.nytimes.com/2026/10/23/insider/cooking-recipes-ai.html) the new features:

> I naïvely assumed A.I. wouldn’t affect my work as a recipe developer and my role at NYT Cooking, where I oversee the editorial side of our recipes and related stories. But as artificial intelligence improved, our product and engineering colleagues saw its potential to help us create features Cooking users wanted.
>
>
> We’ve just launched our latest tool, which gives cooks the ability to apply modifications to our recipes. We’re rolling it out gradually to monitor how it performs (whether it’s working fast enough, for instance) and to see how people are using it (as of now, we’re getting a lot of requests for ingredient substitutions). The tool is currently available to all Cooking subscribers on our iOS app, and we plan to make it available more broadly soon.

The Times had previously rolled out AI features aimed at converting volume-based and weight-based measurements (“What’s one cup of bok choy in grams?”) and scaling a recipe up or down to serve more or fewer people. The main new feature is focused on ingredient substitutions.

Say you’re cooking [braised white beans and greens with parmesan](https://cooking.nytimes.com/recipes/1021902-braised-white-beans-and-greens-with-parmesan), NYT Cooking app in hand. But you notice that you’re out of chard and only have spinach. Cooking veterans know that chard is a rough-and-tumble green that has some backbone[2](https://www.niemanlab.org/2026/10/the-new-york-times-is-adding-more-ai-features-to-its-cooking-app-and-users-arent-thrilled/#rsc-note-2)2 There’s a reason one type of chard is known as “perpetual spinach.”, while spinach is a comparative wimp that will wilt the moment you look at it funny. If you need to sub in spinach for chard, how would the recipe change? Would you, for instance, add the spinach later than you would the chard to account for its pathetic stamina? That’s the sort of thing the new AI feature could account for.

Cooking staffers “spent countless hours evaluating sample after sample to get the chatbot answers to closely align with how we would answer as culinary experts,” Ko writes. “We applied the same rigor as we do to editing, grounded in Times standards.”

But because Ko knows that any AI-powered features are likely to be controversial with a Times audience, she spends quite a lot of space addressing potential objections, everything from “the impact of data centers” to “the concentration of power among A.I. companies” and “the risk of A.I. escaping our control.” These features are designed to enable “the tactile physical pleasure of cooking” and getting a “very real, very human creation” on your table.

Broadly speaking, [commenters](https://www.nytimes.com/2026/10/23/insider/cooking-recipes-ai.html#commentsContainer) weren’t buying it.

“What a massive disappointment,” wrote Susan from New Jersey. “The internet is full of AI cooking content. I pay you because I prefer mine done by people.”

“This decision misses the mark by such a wide margin it’s baffling,” says Ian from Los Angeles. “And the disclosure just as baffling. It would not be inaccurate to summarize the piece as saying ‘I know doing this is bad and I don’t want to be associated with the bad thing so that’s why we are doing the bad thing.'”

“Nobody wants this, it’s bad for cooking, it’s bad for the NYT,” writes Bill from Pittsburgh. “Wasting a column trying to gaslight yourself and your audience into believing that it’s anything but is an embarrassment and a waste of everyone’s time.”

“PLEASE PLEASE PLEASE DO NOT DO THIS,” says Judah Mann of New York. “Oh, wait, you already did. Ok, I’m out.”

Or as Naomi from California puts it: “I am sad that AI has breached the one online resource I truly love.”

Because I enjoy the irony, I scraped the 171 comments left on the Times’ announcement and asked Codex (running GPT-6.1 Sol, at medium thinking) to do some sentiment analysis. (Twelve of the 171 were comments left by Times staffers; I’m excluding them here.) Roughly 77% of the reader comments were negative about the new AI features, it found, versus 14% positive and the remainder neutral or mixed. Among the biggest categories of complaint: This shouldn’t require AI. AI is destroying the environment. AI is not why I’m paying the Times $390 a year. The adjustments the AI produces are going to be bad.

Dozens of commenters asked for a way to turn off the feature. “No, not at this time,” Ko responded, “though this feature is completely optional to use.” Indeed: Don’t ask AI to substitute your chard and AI won’t substitute your chard.

One consistent thread was that cooking is _supposed_ to present you with difficulties and challenges and the whole point is figuring them out by yourself. “Anyone using AI for cooking has no sense of taste and no desire to work out the intricacies of cooking and baking,” writes Michael King from Brooklyn. “To use AI for recipes is beyond the pale. If you are going to use AI, then just cut to the chase and defenestrate yourself.” Or BJ from North Carolina: “So, you’re telling me that I’m too stupid to figure it out on my own?”

Meanwhile, the few positive comments tended to focus on how the AI feature had, in fact, made dietary substitutions easier for them. “I love the new AI feature because it quickly (and so far) accurately converts recipes to gluten free,” Anne Wagner from Kansas City writes. “I don’t cook for stress relief,” says Andy from San Francisco. “I cook to put dinner on the table. Anything that makes the process a little faster or smoother is welcome.”

## Notes

1.   Olives, yecch. [↩](https://www.niemanlab.org/2026/10/the-new-york-times-is-adding-more-ai-features-to-its-cooking-app-and-users-arent-thrilled/#rsc-noteref-1)

articles.content:
Title: The sleep framework: A new way for LLMs to retain knowledge in continual learning

URL Source: https://research.google/blog/the-sleep-framework-a-new-way-for-llms-to-retain-knowledge-in-continual-learning/

Markdown Content:
Modern LLMs achieve impressive performance via pre-training and [in-context learning](https://ai.stanford.edu/blog/understanding-incontext/) (ICL). However, once deployed, they remain largely static, operating with a fixed knowledge cutoff date that leaves them unable to acquire long-term capabilities or adapt to new information.

While updating models with new data seems like the obvious solution, continual parameter updates often trigger [catastrophic forgetting](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Catastrophic_interference), a fundamental issue where learning new tasks severely degrades performance on previously learned ones. Alternatively, relying strictly on ICL limits knowledge retention to the immediate context window: once the context session ends, the acquired short-term information is forgotten.

Inspired by how the human brain processes and stabilizes memory during rest, we introduce a [sleep framework](https://arxiv.org/pdf/2606.03979) in continual learning: a learning paradigm that equips large language models (LLMs) with a continuous _periodic_ lifecycle, enabling them to continually learn, consolidate fragile short-term context into stable long-term parameters. With this framework, we demonstrate that alternating between active interaction and offline memory consolidation allows LLMs to continuously acquire new facts, retain long-context knowledge up to 10M tokens, and improve complex reasoning.

## Rethinking machine learning: Active (wake) vs. sleep phases

Traditional machine learning relies on a strict separation between training and inference. In a continual learning framework, this distinction becomes artificial; an intelligent agent must constantly learn, adapt, and process information.

Under the sleep paradigm, an LLM operates across two primary states:

1.   **Active (wake) phase**: The model actively receives, processes, and interacts with inputs, storing temporary information in fast, short-term memory components.
2.   **Sleep phase**: The model pauses processing new inputs and redirects its internal computations toward memory consolidation and self-improvement.

While terms like "sleep," "dreaming," and "self-improvement" borrow from neuroscience, our framework operates entirely within a fixed model architecture and human-defined training rules. During the offline sleep phase, the model unlocks pre-allocated Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) memory blocks and updates its numerical weights using self-generated practice examples. This automated post-training cycle helps a deployed model absorb new facts and sharpen its reasoning accuracy while keeping its core codebase and design unchanged.

## Key components of the sleep process

The sleep paradigm addresses catastrophic forgetting and continuous adaptation through two stages: memory consolidation and dreaming.

### 1. Memory consolidation

In the human brain, [non-rapid eye movement](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Non-rapid_eye_movement_sleep) (NREM) slow-wave sleep consolidates fragile memories into long-term structures via abstraction and distillation. Our proposed sleep framework mirrors this natural phenomenon through two key technical mechanisms:

*   **Parameter expansion & continuum memory hierarchy:** To prevent catastrophic forgetting, the model dynamically scales its capacity during sleep. Using a [Mixture of Experts](https://huggingface.co/blog/moe) (MoE) and [Hope](https://arxiv.org/abs/2512.24695) architecture , newly unlocked, low-rank experts are integrated into stable, lower-frequency memory blocks to store incoming knowledge without disrupting older parameters.
*   **Knowledge seeding (upward distillation):** Fragile short-term memories stored in high-frequency layers (e.g., in-context memory) are transferred into the newly expanded long-term parameters. This is achieved through [Generalized Knowledge Distillation](https://huggingface.co/docs/trl/en/gkd_trainer) (GKD) combined with [reinforcement learning](https://www.geeksforgeeks.org/machine-learning/what-is-reinforcement-learning/) (RL)-based [imitation learning](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Imitation_learning):
    *   **On-policy distillation:** The expanded student model learns token-specific feedback from teacher distributions generated on self-sampled sequences.
    *   **Learning to imitate (LTI):** The student model is rewarded based on semantic and absolute similarity ([Levenshtein distance](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Levenshtein_distance)) when completing prefixes of teacher-generated text.

*   **Synaptic pruning:** Once the memory consolidation into lower-frequency modules is complete, the high-frequency temporary parameters are reset, freeing up capacity for future active sessions.

### 2. Dreaming for self-improvement

During [REM sleep](https://www.thensf.org/what-is-rem-sleep/), the human brain actively simulates scenarios, consolidates emotional/semantic connections, and explores novel neural pathways. Mirroring this, during the “dreaming stage”, the sleep framework implements an autonomous self-improvement loop:

*   **Random expert selection:** During synthetic data generation, the MoE router randomly activates non-standard experts. This forces the model to mix disparate domains of knowledge and uncover latent patterns.
*   **Curated rehearsal:** The model generates synthetic training samples ("dreams") and filters them using gradient-based data selection to prioritize samples with the highest potential to boost overall model capability.
*   **RL refinement:** The model performs supervised fine-tuning on top-rated dream samples and evaluates whether the generation improves performance on downstream tasks.

## Theoretical foundations

Beyond the empirical results, our sleep paradigm is grounded in a theory that clarifies why its two stages (memory consolidation and dreaming) can support continual learning without simply trading new knowledge for old capabilities.

For memory consolidation, the analysis shows that knowledge seeding can be understood as a structured, low-rank compression problem. The model is not asked to copy every detail of its short-term traces into its parameters. Instead, it identifies a compact set of directions that best preserve both the model’s own on-policy behavior and the semantic qualities rewarded by the learning objective.

This perspective explains the complementary roles of the two signals: on-policy distillation aligns consolidation with the trajectories the model will actually produce at inference time, reducing the mismatch that can arise when training only on teacher-generated distributions; meanwhile, the semantic reward changes what is worth retaining, prioritizing directions that preserve meaning and task-relevant behavior rather than merely matching token probabilities. Parameter expansion then provides the capacity needed to write these selected memories without overwriting previously consolidated knowledge.

For dreaming, the theory characterizes random expert activation and reward-based sample selection as mechanisms for improving the geometry of learning. Injecting different MoEs broadens the set of gradient directions explored during synthetic generation, exposing the model to a richer collection of updates than those induced by its ordinary wake-time data alone. Gradient-based filtering then emphasizes the synthetic experiences that carry the most useful learning signal, strengthening informative directions while preserving the structure of the underlying gradient space.

Together, these steps yield a more balanced optimization landscape: learning is less dominated by a small number of directions, gradients are better conditioned, and the model can make more stable progress when refining its capabilities. In this view, dreaming is not simply self-generated data augmentation; it is a deliberate process for diversifying, selecting, and consolidating the updates through which the model improves itself.

For [continual translation](https://arxiv.org/abs/2512.24695), in unseen languages, such as Manchu and Kalamang, the sleep framework maintained a near-zero performance drop in multi-stage evaluations, whereas standard baselines like ICL, [Cartridges](https://arxiv.org/abs/2506.06266), and [supervised fine-tuning](https://cameronrwolfe.substack.com/p/understanding-and-using-supervised) (SFT) suffered severe catastrophic forgetting during sequential learning.

In long-context understanding on the [BABILong](https://arxiv.org/abs/2406.10149) benchmark, our sleep method demonstrated near-perfect scaling up to 10M tokens, outperforming strong baselines like [GPT-4](http://openai.com/index/gpt-4-research/), and [Titans](https://research.google/blog/titans-miras-helping-ai-have-long-term-memory/) by using sleep-time consolidation to compress long-context information directly into parametric memory.

For factual knowledge incorporation evaluated on [SQuAD](https://deepeval.com/docs/benchmarks-squad) and [continued pre-training](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/nova/latest/userguide/nova-cpt.html) (CPT), our sleep method achieved 48.9% on single-task and 46.2% on CPT evaluations, outperforming baseline methods including the base model, SFT, and [Self-Adapting Language Models](https://arxiv.org/abs/2506.10943) (SEAL) by successfully integrating new factual information without degrading existing model representations.

Finally, on mathematical reasoning benchmarks including [AIME 24/25](https://artificialanalysis.ai/evaluations/aime-2025) and[HMMT 25](https://intuitionlabs.ai/articles/hmmt25-ai-benchmark-explained), sleep-enhanced base-model achieved accuracy scores of 79.2%, 69.0%, and 46.1%, respectively. This outperformed baselines like SFT, group relative policy optimization (GRPO), and on-policy self-distillation (OPSD), showing that pairing memory consolidation with imitation learning drives superior reasoning performance.

## Conclusion

Our sleep paradigm provides a path toward autonomous, continually learning AI systems. By moving beyond static pre-training and fragile context windows, alternating between active learning and offline rest empowers LLMs to retain short-term memories, abstract new skills into long-term parameter structures, and continuously self-improve without catastrophic forgetting.

Markdown Content:
## Code of Conduct

This is largely taken from [Zig's Code of Conduct](https://ziglang.org/code-of-conduct/).

The rules here are strict. This space is for focused, on topic, technical work on the MicroZig and Zig Embedded Group projects only. It is everyone’s responsibility to maintain a positive environment, especially when disagreements occur.

This document applies to the Zig Embedded Group GitHub organization and Discord server.

## Strict No LLM / No AI Policy

This policy takes effect October 28th, 2026.

No LLM-generated content, whether it be code or prose.

No paraphrasing LLM-generated content.

No LLMs for editing, including fixing spelling or grammatical errors.

No LLMs for translation. English is encouraged, but not required. You are welcome to post in your native language and rely on others to have their own translation tools of choice to interpret your words.

No LLMs for brainstorming and then sharing the results of that brainstorming, even if you create the prose. If you use a chatbot to give you advice on a comment on the issue tracker, that comment is unwelcome.

No LLMs for finding bugs.

No talking about use of chatbot/LLM services.

## Safe, Constructive Behavior Only

Examples of behavior that contribute to creating a positive environment include:

*   Using welcoming and inclusive language.
*   Being respectful of differing viewpoints and experiences.
*   Gracefully accepting constructive criticism.
*   Helping another person accomplish their own goals.
*   Showing empathy towards others.
*   Showing appreciation for others’ work.
*   Validating someone else’s experience, skills, insight, and use cases.

Examples of unacceptable behavior by participants include:

*   Unwelcome sexual attention or advances, or use of sexualized language or imagery that causes discomfort.
*   Trolling, insulting/derogatory comments, and personal attacks. Anything antagonistic towards someone else.
*   Off-topic discussion of any kind - especially offensive or sensitive issues.
*   Publishing others’ private information, such as a physical or electronic address, without explicit permission.
*   Discussing this Code of Conduct or publicly accusing someone of violating it.
*   Making someone else feel like an outsider or implying a lack of technical abilities.
*   Destructive behavior. Anything that harms MicroZig or another open-source project.

## Enforcement

If you need to report an issue you can contact Matthew Knight and Felix Queißner. We will swiftly remove anyone who is antagonizing others or being generally destructive.

This includes Private Harassment. If person A is directly harassed or antagonized by person B, person B will be blocked from participating in this space even if the harassment didn’t take place on one of the mediums directly under rule of this Code of Conduct.

As noted, discussing this Code of Conduct should not take place on GitHub, or Discord, because these spaces are for directly working on code, not for meta-discussion. If you have any issues with it, you can contact me directly, or you can join one of the community spaces that has different rules.

Matthew Knight [mattnite@proton.me](mailto:mattnite@proton.me)

## Conclusion

Thanks for reading the rules. Together, we can make this space welcoming and inclusive for everyone, regardless of age, body size, disability, ethnicity, sex characteristics, gender identity and expression, level of experience, education, socio-economic status, nationality, personal appearance, race, religion, or sexual identity and orientation.
